{{Short description|On prime divisors of differences two nth powers}}
In [[number theory]], '''Zsigmondy's theorem''', named after [[Karl Zsigmondy]], states that if <math>a>b>0</math> are [[coprime]] [[integer]]s, then for any integer <math>n \ge 1</math>, there is a [[prime number]] ''p'' (called a ''primitive prime divisor'') that divides <math>a^n-b^n</math> and does not divide <math>a^k-b^k</math> for any positive integer <math>k<n</math>, with the following exceptions:

*<math>n=1</math>, <math>a-b=1</math>; then <math>a^n-b^n=1</math> which has no prime divisors
*<math>n=2</math>, <math>a+b</math> a [[power of two]]; then any [[parity (mathematics)|odd]] prime factors of  <math>a^2-b^2=(a+b)(a^1-b^1)</math> must be contained in <math>a^1-b^1</math>, which is also [[parity (mathematics)|even]]
*<math>n=6</math>, <math>a=2</math>, <math>b=1</math>; then <math>a^6-b^6=63=3^2\times 7=(a^2-b^2)^2 (a^3-b^3)</math>

This generalizes Bang's theorem,<ref>{{cite journal|title = Taltheoretiske Undersøgelser|author = A. S. Bang|journal = Tidsskrift for Mathematik|series = 5|volume = 4|pages = 70–80|year = 1886|jstor = 24539988|publisher = Mathematica Scandinavica}} And {{cite journal|title = Taltheoretiske Undersøgelser (continued, see p. 80)|journal = Tidsskrift for Mathematik|volume = 4|pages = 130–137|jstor = 24540006|last1 = Bang|first1 = A. S.|year = 1886}}</ref> which states that if <math>n>1</math> and <math>n</math> is not equal to 6, then <math>2^n-1</math> has a prime divisor not dividing any <math>2^k-1</math> with <math>k<n</math>.

Similarly, <math>a^n+b^n</math> has at least one primitive prime divisor with the exception <math>2^3+1^3=9</math>.

Zsigmondy's theorem is often useful, especially in [[group theory]], where it is used to [[mathematical proof|prove]] that various [[group (mathematics)|groups]] have distinct [[order of a group|orders]] except when they are known to be the same. <ref>Montgomery, H. "[https://listserv.nodak.edu/cgi-bin/wa.exe?A2=NMBRTHRY;51c82f9a.0109&S= Divisibility of Mersenne Numbers.]" 17 Sep 2001.</ref><ref>{{cite journal
| last       = Artin
| first      = Emil
| author-link= Emil Artin
| date       = August 1955
| title      = The Orders of the Linear Groups
| journal    = [[Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics|Comm. Pure Appl. Math.]]
| volume     = 8
| issue      = 3
| pages      = 355–365
| doi        = 10.1002/cpa.3160080302
}}</ref> It is also used in [[Mathematical olympiad|mathematical olympiads]].

==History==
The [[theorem]] was discovered by [[Karl Zsigmondy]] who proved it in 1892.

== Generalizations ==
Let <math>(a_n)_{n\ge1}</math> be a [[sequence]] of nonzero integers.
The '''Zsigmondy set''' associated to the sequence is the [[set (mathematics)|set]]

:<math>\mathcal{Z}(a_n) = \{n \ge 1 : a_n \text{ has no primitive prime divisors}\}.</math>

i.e., the set of indices <math>n</math> such that every prime dividing <math>a_n</math> also divides some <math>a_m</math> for some <math>m < n</math>. Thus Zsigmondy's theorem implies that <math>\mathcal{Z}(a^n-b^n)\subset\{1,2,6\}</math>, and [[Carmichael's theorem]] says that the Zsigmondy set of the [[Fibonacci sequence]] is <math>\{1,2,6,12\}</math>, and that of the [[Pell sequence]] is <math>\{1\}</math>. In 2001 Bilu, Hanrot, and Voutier<ref>Y. Bilu, G. Hanrot, P.M. Voutier, Existence of primitive divisors of Lucas and Lehmer numbers, ''J. Reine Angew. Math.'' '''539''' (2001), 75-122</ref>
proved that in general, if <math>(a_n)_{n\ge1}</math> is a [[Lucas sequence]] or a [[Lehmer number|Lehmer sequence]], then <math>\mathcal{Z}(a_n) \subseteq \{ 1 \le n \le 30 \}</math> (see {{oeis|id=A285314}}, there are only 13 such <math>n</math>s, namely 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 12, 13, 18, 30).
Lucas and Lehmer sequences are examples of [[divisibility sequence]]s.

It is also known that if <math>(W_n)_{n\ge1}</math> is an [[elliptic divisibility sequence]], then its Zsigmondy
set <math>\mathcal{Z}(W_n)</math> is [[finite set|finite]].<ref>[[Joseph H. Silverman|J.H. Silverman]],
Wieferich's criterion and the ''abc''-conjecture,
''J. Number Theory'' '''30''' (1988), 226-237</ref> However, the result is ineffective in the sense that the proof does not give an explicit [[upper bound]] for the largest element in <math>\mathcal{Z}(W_n)</math>,
although it is possible to give an effective upper bound for the number of elements in <math>\mathcal{Z}(W_n)</math>.<ref>P. Ingram, J.H. Silverman, Uniform estimates for primitive divisors in elliptic divisibility sequences, ''Number theory, Analysis and Geometry'', Springer-Verlag, 2010, 233-263.</ref>
